analysis.one_liner: Directs the EPA to regulate all PFAS 'forever chemicals' as hazardous air pollutants.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had Republican and Democratic cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Environmental Protection Agency to add every PFAS chemical — man-made 'forever chemicals' with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom — to the Clean Air Act's list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days, and then to identify the major and area sources of PFAS air emissions within a year [S2] [S3]. That listing is the trigger for federal emission-control standards on industrial facilities that release these chemicals into the air. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or work near facilities that emit PFAS chemicals into the air — including communities around chemical plants, galvanizing operations, and other industrial sources — would gain a federal requirement that those emissions be identified and controlled [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Within 180 days of enactment, the EPA would have to issue a final rule adding all PFAS with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom to the Clean Air Act's list of hazardous air pollutants, treating them as a class rather than chemical-by-chemical [S3] [S2].

Within 365 days after that rule, the EPA would have to revise its source list to include the categories of major and area sources that emit PFAS, which is the step that sets up emission standards for industrial facilities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial facilities that release PFAS into the air would bear the cost of emission controls once the EPA sets standards for these newly listed hazardous pollutants [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial PFAS emitters and chemical makers

drawbacks.text: Adding PFAS as a class would impose air-emission controls on many industries at once — including producers of fluorinated compounds used in semiconductors, refrigerants, and pharmaceuticals — a broad compliance cost that critics could argue outpaces the evidence for harm from every individual chemical in the class [S3].

A statutory deadline forcing the EPA to list PFAS within 180 days would leave little room for the agency's usual chemical-by-chemical risk assessment, raising the prospect of contested rules and litigation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real and growing public-health concern: PFAS are man-made chemicals that persist in the environment and may have adverse human health effects [S2]. The cost is concentrated on industrial emitters who would need new controls, and the design choice to regulate the entire class at once trades speed and completeness against the precision of chemical-by-chemical analysis. The bill's substance was never tested in a hearing or amendment process, so those tradeoffs were never debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) introduced the bill on March 17, 2022, with original cosponsors from both parties: Reps. Bill Posey (R-FL), Debbie Dingell (D-MI), Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that emit PFAS chemicals into the air — chemical manufacturers and other industrial sources — are better off, since they avoided the emission-control standards the bill would have set in motion.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 2 of its 4 cosponsors were Republicans — but it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show a partisan split.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers of PFAS and fluorinated compounds
industries.note: Listing all PFAS as hazardous air pollutants would have exposed these producers and major industrial emitters to Clean Air Act emission-control standards, a direct cost. Blocking the bill preserved the status quo in which PFAS air emissions face no such class-wide controls.

industries.industry: Other industrial PFAS emitters (e.g., galvanizing, semiconductor, and coating operations)
industries.note: The bill required the EPA to identify major and area sources of PFAS air emissions, the first step toward mandatory emission standards for these facilities; the bill's death leaves their air emissions unregulated as a class.
